data.title: Man arrested after allegedly refusing to share HK$30m Mark Six prize with group
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested a 36-year-old man suspected of having fled with a Mark Six jackpot worth around HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) that he should have shared with 14 colleagues.
A source said on Friday that a 53-year-old man had reported to police on Wednesday that he was one of 15 colleagues who had chipped in to buy a Mark Six ticket for the draw on Saturday.
The group reportedly comprised some staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD).
His colleague, a 36-year-old man, bought the ticket and held the account into which the winnings were paid, the source said.
After the ticket won, the 36-year-old refused to evenly divide the prize money among the group, which prompted a dispute, the insider said.
A meeting was held on Wednesday evening in Aberdeen to try to resolve the dispute, but the source said the ticket-buyer allegedly insisted that he would not split the winnings during the roughly 30-minute negotiation.
Worried that the 36-year-old intended to keep the entire prize and disappear, the 53-year-old man filed a police report at 10.06pm the same day.
The 36-year-old reportedly did not go to work for five days.
Police said on Friday night that a man, 36, had been arrested on suspicion of theft. He remained in custody.
Officers from Western police district are handling the investigation.
In response to South China Morning Post queries, the FEHD said it noted that police were investigating the case and would cooperate with their probe.
“As the police investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for the department to comment on the details at this stage,” a department spokesman said.
The September 5 draw was a “Mark Six 50th Anniversary Snowball” draw, held by the Hong Kong Jockey Club, with a record jackpot of HK$228 million.
According to the club’s website, the first prize pool had 3.5 winning units, each paying HK$63.3 million.

data.title: ‘Pillar of Shame’ sculptor to ask Denmark to negotiate for artwork’s return
data.description:
The creator of a sculpture commemorating those killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown will ask Danish authorities to negotiate with Hong Kong for its return, with city officials disputing his claims of owning the confiscated artwork.
The fate of the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture has come back under the spotlight after the High Court on Friday handed jail sentences to three former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China at the end of a high-profile national security trial.
In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Danish artist Jens Galschiot said he intended to ask his government to officially declare the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) sculpture a work of art and part of his country’s cultural heritage so it could be returned to “its rightful owner”.
He revealed he had raised the issue with the Danish parliament’s foreign policy committee, adding that a cross-party group of the European Parliament and the European Union’s Hong Kong office had also followed up on the matter.
“For me, the issue is quite simple: the ‘Pillar of Shame’ is my sculpture,” Galschiot said.
“It was never given away. It should not be confiscated or destroyed because of its political symbolism or because it commemorates the victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre.”
In its verdict last month, the court found the now-disbanded alliance had incited supporters to undermine the Communist Party’s leadership by advocating the group’s operational objective of ending “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

The three presiding judges found the alliance had organised various public events to achieve that aim, including the annual cleaning of the sculpture at the University of Hong Kong campus.
The court has adjourned a decision on the sculpture’s disposal, pending the hearing of further arguments.
Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-wah of the force’s national security department rejected Galschiot’s claim of ownership on Friday and said the sculpture belonged to the alliance, whose properties were now under the official receiver’s jurisdiction.
Without mentioning the sculpture by its name, Li said “this pillar” was closely linked to the alliance’s attempts to incite others to undermine the Communist Party.
“I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” he said.
Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung added that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated.
Former alliance vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung, who was sentenced to seven years and three months in jail on Friday, had demanded that the sculpture be returned to Galschiot.
But the court said she might not be in a position to comment since she did not act on behalf of the alliance during the trial.
The judges nonetheless invited Chow to make written submissions on the matter, but added she should also include reasons why she was a relevant party.
The alliance was best known for organising annual candlelight vigils to mark Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters on June 4, 1989. The event used to be the only large-scale commemoration of the incident on Chinese soil.

data.title: ‘Rest in eternal peace’: veteran horror actor, filmmaker Simon Loui dies at age 62
data.description:
Veteran Hong Kong actor and filmmaker Simon Loui Yu-yeung, better known to fans as the “King of Ghosts” for his prolific work in horror films, has died at the age of 62.
Long-time friend and fellow actor Frankie Ng Chi-hung revealed to reporters on Friday that Loui’s wife, TV and radio personality Ma Li, had confirmed the filmmaker had died in a hospital in Guangzhou on Monday after losing his battle with gastric cancer.
“The family hoped to stay low profile. There was no big announcement,” Ng said. “May he rest in eternal peace, free from all pain and sickness in heaven.”
Ng said he had known of Loui’s previous struggles with gastric cancer, which had been treated, but later learned the condition had come back in recent years.
Loui was born in 1964 and enjoyed an entertainment career spanning more than three decades across TV, radio and film and included his work as a filmmaker.
After finishing an artist training course at free-to-air broadcaster TVB in the late 1980s, he started with appearances in TV dramas and variety shows before moving to the film industry in the early 1990s.

The jump saw him quickly become a familiar face among fans of Hong Kong’s horror and comedy genres.
Loui appeared in nearly 100 films over the course of his career, with notable credits including the comedy dramas Play with Strangers (2000) and Headlines (2001).
But the entertainer earned his title as the “King of Ghosts” for his appearances in the long-running comedy horror series Troublesome Night, starring in numerous instalments throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Loui also co-wrtote the action-thriller The Replacement Suspects (2001).
Aside from TV and film, he tried his hand at radio. During the 1990s and 2000s, he also hosted a series of late-night horror programmes on Metro Radio and Commercial Radio.
But the performer had largely stepped back from the limelight since marrying mainland Chinese personality Ma in 2012.
The couple had a son together and settled in Guangzhou, with Loui rarely returning to Hong Kong.

data.title: Man dies in fall from scaffolding in 19th fatal construction accident this year
data.description:
A construction worker has died after falling while erecting scaffolding, marking Hong Kong’s 19th fatal accident in the construction industry and second to involve truss-out platforms this year, according to police and a concern group.
The force said it received a report at 11.39am on Friday that a male worker had fallen and was found lying on a podium along Yu Chau Street in Sham Shui Po.
The man was rushed to the nearby Caritas Medical Centre, where he was later declared dead. Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, with the exact cause of death to be determined by an autopsy.
The Labour Department said it had immediately deployed staff to the scene upon receiving the report, adding that it was investigating the cause of the incident.
Fay Siu Sin-man, chief executive of the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims, said the victim was a 50-year-old sub-subcontractor who had worked as a scaffolder for many years.
The man arrived at the site at around 8am and was putting up his second set of scaffolding when a support bracket was suspected to have come loose, causing him to fall, she said.
She added that the building had suffered from water leakage, and that the scaffolding was being erected to allow for inspections and repairs.
Siu said the man left behind two adult children – a son who was a student and a daughter who was unemployed.
“I feel very grieved about the accident, but it also reflects just how severe and frequent workplace accidents have become,” she said.
Siu noted that it was the 19th fatal accident in the construction industry this year and the second such incident to involve truss-out scaffolds.
The first such accident occurred in February, when a 57-year-old worker fell to his death while setting up scaffolding on the exterior wall of a Maxim’s Group food factory in Tai Po. The case was also classified as an industrial accident.
The association at the time urged frontline workers to ensure their own safety and said employers should also provide suitable equipment, such as safety belts, and monitor employees working at height to ensure they used the gear properly.
Siu said on Friday that she hoped the employer, the main contractor and the subcontractor involved in the latest case could make proper arrangements to support the family.
She also urged the man’s employer and the relevant authorities to seriously review how to prevent such accidents.

data.title: Ant to let AI agents shop via 10 digital wallets, from AlipayHK to Starryblu
data.description:
Ant International, the overseas affiliate of Chinese fintech giant Ant Group, is making a major bid to power the next phase of mobile payments: letting autonomous artificial intelligence agents handle your electronic wallet to make purchases.
The company on Friday open-sourced its Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) on GitHub, effectively putting it forward as a potential global technical standard for how AI agents securely pay for real-world goods.
AMP was built onto Ant International’s existing Alipay+ cross-border network, which connects to 10 major Asian digital wallets serving 1.5 billion consumer accounts for an initial phase, according to the company.
The protocol’s release would “enable agents to enter existing mobile payment systems as trusted actors”, allowing platforms like Alipay in mainland China, AlipayHK in Hong Kong, Starryblu in Singapore, and KakaoPay or Toss in South Korea to accelerate their AI strategies, said Yang Jiang-ming, Ant International’s chief innovation officer.
Beyond Asia, Ant International on Thursday also announced a joint effort with credit card giants Visa and Mastercard on a so-called know-your-agent (KYA) framework, an effort to establish standardised identity verification for AI agents across card networks, digital wallets and online marketplaces globally, the company said.
The launches come as tech firms increasingly focus on autonomous AI agents capable of carrying out end-to-end commercial tasks.
Speaking at a conference in Shanghai this week, Ant Group CEO Cyril Han Xinyi said that many Chinese merchants still struggled to adapt their services into formats AI agents could navigate, limiting their participation in the emerging agent economy.
Spun off in 2024, Ant International aims to build the world’s largest agentic AI payment network. Its Alipay+ network, launched in 2020, has connected more than 150 million merchants to over 2 billion user accounts across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Latin America.

In July, Ant International raised about US$1.2 billion to accelerate international growth in its first known funding round, with existing backers Ant Group and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – taking part.
To address consumer privacy and security risks tied to automated spending, the company said AMP included an AgentSafePay feature, which offered merchants a money-back guarantee to cover potential losses related to agent-initiated transactions.
The protocol also established “clear boundaries of permissions” so consumers could retain ultimate control over their accounts, the company said.

data.title: Over 60% of new dentists join Department of Health after mandatory internship
data.description:
About 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s first batch of dental graduates who underwent mandatory internship training have joined the city’s Department of Health, a move that has helped “significantly ease” the manpower crunch.
The development followed a controversial amendment to the Dentists Registration Ordinance in 2024, requiring all dental graduates in Hong Kong to complete a 12-month internship before obtaining a full licence starting in 2025. The measure aimed to enhance hands-on clinical experience in real-life settings.
Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant-in-charge of the department’s dental services, said on Friday that the government had recruited 62 per cent, or 46 of the first batch of 75 interns.
The rest went on to work at the Prince Philip Dental Hospital’s teaching facility, at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), in non-governmental organisations or in the private sector.
“While students have learned a lot from their six-year undergraduate training, the internship allowed them to put what they learned in books into practice in the real world, meeting different kinds of patients in different roles under the support of experienced dentists,” Hse said.
“During the internship, they never know what kind of problems will be brought into the room by the next patients, which is different from their clinical training at school … that could enhance their clinical judgment and independent thinking skills.”
Under the internship, all students were rotated to four clinical settings – general and emergency dental service, public hospital, teaching hospital, and school or community dental service – with each rotation lasting for three months.
Participants were subject to ongoing assessments by veteran dentists.
After completing the internship, students were issued with a certificate of experience by the Dental Council of Hong Kong on August 31, followed by full registration the following day.
All students passed the internship, except for one who was suspended from duty in January for accessing the digital medical records of 16 patients without consent.
Hse said the department would build on the experience and continue the rotational arrangement in the future, while increasing their exposure to different specialities and their safety awareness when using the digital health record systems and social media.

In an anonymous online survey that covered about 70 per cent of dental interns in July, more than 80 per cent said they were satisfied with the internship arrangement.
Reasons cited included the constructive and prompt feedback they received from senior dentists, alongside opportunities to enhance their communication, clinical and time-management skills.
Patients also gave positive feedback to those interns.
Dr Sharon Lee Siu-man, a consultant dental surgeon at the department, said that while the purpose of the new rule was never intended to fill vacancies in the public sector, the manpower crunch had been “significantly eased”.
“We will continue to run the internship programme, ensure sufficient roles for them to complete the internship, and that is not related to our manpower situation at all.”
HKU, the city’s sole dental school, supplies about 70 new dentists each year. But most graduates tend to join the private sector, which offers better pay and hours.
Health authorities earlier predicted that Hong Kong would be short of 180 dentists by 2030 and 120 by 2035, before seeing a surplus of 20 by 2040.
Dr Jason Yip, a graduate who just completed the internship and joined the department as a dental officer, said the undergraduate training had already equipped graduates with certain skills.
“Throughout the six years of studies, we started clinical internship by the end of year two, and many more treatments were performed in the third year … we needed to meet a certain number of [teeth treated] to graduate in the first place,” he said.
Yip added that the internship taught him that being a dentist was not just about performing treatments, but also “perfecting the details”.
He recalled an elderly lady with acute tooth pain who requested removable dentures, but wished to keep them discreet so people around her would not know.
He struggled to find a solution until a veteran specialist guided him, and the patient was happy with the result.

data.title: Why Hong Kong banks see mainland Chinese investors as key to wealth growth
data.description:
Hong Kong banks expect the contribution of mainland Chinese investors to the city’s wealth management business to continue to grow through 2030, presenting opportunities despite Beijing’s tightened cross-border tax rules.
Mainland China’s share of local assets under management was projected to reach 68 per cent from 59 per cent within five years, according to a report released by the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB) and Deloitte China on Friday.
The report surveyed 147 member banks in the first half of 2026 and offered 37 recommendations on the sector’s development as Hong Kong prepares to unveil its first five-year plan.
“Hong Kong has become the world’s largest cross-border wealth management centre [and] will continue to serve as a vital platform linking mainland China with international capital,” said Stephen Chan, acting chairman of HKAB and deputy CEO of Bank of China (Hong Kong), at a media briefing on Friday.
Surveyed banks considered wealth management to be the biggest growth driver, said David Wu, Hong Kong financial services industry leader at Deloitte China.
Rising demand from mainland investors for international diversification, intergenerational wealth transfer and the expanding family office sector were the primary factors, according to the report.
Banks that integrated portfolio construction, family governance, succession planning and digital asset custody would be best positioned to capitalise on this growth, HKAB and Deloitte said.
To seize opportunities from mainland China, lenders urged the Hong Kong government to enhance the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect Scheme by gradually relaxing investor eligibility, easing sales and promotion rules, raising quotas and broadening product ranges to include medium-risk and higher-return options.
Wealth Management Connect, launched in 2021, is currently open only to Hongkongers as well as mainland residents in the Greater Bay Area, an economic region that includes Hong Kong, Macau and nine mainland cities in southern China’s Guangdong province.
Eligible mainland investors should have at least two years of investment experience as well as a minimum of 1 million yuan (US$150,000) in net financial assets and 2 million yuan in household financial assets.
Banks also advised the government to deepen financial linkages with mainland China by adding a long-awaited connect scheme for initial public offerings. They urged accelerating the inclusion of a yuan counter in Stock Connect, enabling mainland investors to subscribe to new listings in the city while boosting yuan internationalisation.
The recommendations came as Beijing tightened taxation on cross-border gains of mainland residents and beneficiaries from offshore trusts and insurance, sparking concerns over Hong Kong’s financial industry.
However, Beijing has backed Hong Kong’s role as an international asset and wealth management centre, enshrined in the country’s latest five-year plan through 2030.
Beyond wealth management, the lenders also highlighted the integration of the bay area corridor and artificial intelligence deployment as two other pillars for the next five years.
They suggested promoting yuan usage in Belt and Road Initiative projects to drive the internationalisation of the currency and establishing a quantum computing strategy to secure Hong Kong’s long-term competitiveness.

data.title: Treasury yield hits 19-year high, ECB raises rates: the numbers moving markets
data.description:
China’s buoyant stock market lifted brokers’ earnings in the first half, while Hong Kong saw continued growth in retirement assets. Beyond China, a strengthening yen and Washington’s Treasury buy-back programme highlighted shifting dynamics in global currency and bond markets.
Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week.
Chinese brokerage revenue jumps more than 50 per cent
Chinese brokerages saw revenue from their core business rise by more than 50 per cent in the first half, as buoyant A-share trading lifted commission income.
The broader industry also benefited from the market rally, with 150 brokerages reporting a 23.5 per cent average increase in net profit as operating revenue climbed 31 per cent, according to the Securities Association of China.
Hong Kong’s MPF assets reach HK$1.67 trillion
Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund has amassed HK$1.67 trillion in assets as of end-June, as policymakers consider widening the investment options available to the city’s compulsory retirement scheme.
The Financial Services Development Council has proposed allowing part of the fund to invest in alternative assets and infrastructure, while calling for Hong Kong to attract more long-term mainland capital to invest globally through the city.
Japanese yen strengthens to seven-month high of 153.63 per US dollar
The Japanese yen strengthened to 153.63 against the US dollar on Wednesday, its strongest level since February, as expectations of tighter monetary policy by the Bank of Japan supported the currency.
Expectations that government efforts could encourage Japanese investors to bring overseas assets home, generating increased demand for the yen, have also fuelled the rally.
US 30-year Treasury yield hits 19-year high at 5.37 per cent
The US 30-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.37 per cent on Thursday, its highest level since 2007, as a global bond sell-off intensified amid mounting concerns over inflation and US government debt.
The surge came even as the US Treasury stepped up efforts to support the market, buying back about US$5.2 billion of 10- to 20-year bonds on Thursday. However, the amount fell short of its US$6 billion maximum announced earlier, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose to around 4.95 per cent after the operation.
ECB raises rates by 25 basis points to tame inflation
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points on Thursday, taking its benchmark deposit rate to 2.5 per cent in its second rate increase this year.
The ECB said inflation was expected to remain well above its 2 per cent target for an extended period, as the Middle East conflict continued to push up energy prices. It expected headline inflation to average 3 per cent this year and 2.5 per cent in 2027.

data.title: ‘The more, the better’: Hong Kong won’t cap talent passes, labour chief says
data.description:
The Hong Kong government will not cap the number of admissions under its talent schemes, with the labour minister saying “the more, the better” amid a global race for skilled workers, despite rising concerns over whether the city can absorb the influx.
Wrapping up a five-day visit to Hong Kong by overseas innovation and technology specialists, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that no quota would be set for the two main categories of talent passes – one for professionals with job offers and the Top Talent Pass Scheme – but renewals were conditional on holders being employed or having set up companies in the city.
“Such requirements ensure arrivals contribute meaningfully to the economy. The more talent that comes to Hong Kong, the better,” he said.
Experts have raised concerns about whether the city can absorb the influx of non-local talent without putting strains on its population.
Hong Kong has rolled out a suite of talent schemes since late 2022, including the Top Talent Pass Scheme for top earners and graduates of leading universities, the points-based Quality Migrant Admission Scheme, and channels for professionals with job offers and technology specialists.
Authorities have approved 126,942 applications since 2023, with 94.5 per cent, or 120,009, coming from mainland China.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu will deliver the 2026 policy address and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan next Wednesday.
The address is expected to include an update to the city’s talent list, as the government reportedly moves to add AI-related professions and fold AI qualifications into existing entries to ease an anticipated shortage of interdisciplinary AI experts, with work slated for completion in the first half of 2027.

A delegation of 20 overseas tech specialists organised by Hong Kong Talent Engage (HKTE), a government office under the Labour and Welfare Bureau, concluded a five-day visit from Monday covering Hong Kong, Qianhai in Shenzhen and Nansha in Guangzhou.
The tour aimed to familiarise participants with the region’s innovation and technology ecosystem and support measures.
The group comprised winners of a hackathon co-organised by HKTE and Germany’s EuroTech Federation in June, and federation representatives.
They toured major tech hubs including Cyberport, Hong Kong Science Park and the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, as well as the Northern Metropolis, meeting local research institutes, enterprises and start-ups to explore opportunities in artificial intelligence, robotics, smart transport and biotechnology.
Cem Deniz Araz, a German doctor and chief executive of heal.health, a preventive healthcare start-up, said he was impressed by the Greater Bay Area’s hi-tech infrastructure. His company, which is still in early development, was exploring opportunities to expand in Hong Kong and mainland China.
“What impressed me most was the self-driving technology – I never saw that in Germany,” he said.
“Hong Kong also has great potential for my AI healthcare business, as the city is dealing with an ageing population.”

Aleksandr Gorbunov, a Russian co-founder of muunai, an AI start-up focused on automating clinical documentation for medical practices, said he was struck by the scale of robotics manufacturing on the mainland, and hoped to explore opportunities there in the future.
“We got to visit biotech, AI and robotics at the forefront of development in China,” he said.
“At one robotics company, they showed us what their robots can do, and seeing that as a human was truly remarkable.”

data.title: ‘Freaked out’: why AI safety fears are spiking ahead of Xi-Trump summit
data.description:
A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China.
The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg.
OpenAI may coordinate the slowdown with other leading AI laboratories, though some firms may decline to participate, the report said, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Altman’s remarks underscored a growing reckoning in Silicon Valley over the risks of rapid AI advancement.
[Industry leaders are] racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives
Julie Steele, OpenAI
Paul Christiano, a prominent AI safety researcher who recently joined OpenAI’s non-profit board to serve on its safety and security committee, warned on Thursday of a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term” based on the current trajectory of the technology.
In a Thursday post on X that drew more than 1.5 million views and 10,000 likes, OpenAI safety team member Julie Steele wrote in a personal capacity: “I also think we need to slow down.”
Steele cited a viral post from former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon, who said earlier this week that he had resigned from Anthropic because both industry leaders were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.
Political momentum is also building. US Senator Bernie Sanders pledged on Thursday to introduce legislation to “pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether”.
Safety alarms intensify at US labs
The urgency behind these warnings has been heightened by growing security breaches and monitoring difficulties across the industry.
Anthropic said on Wednesday that an early version of its flagship Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorised access to a third-party computer system during testing in January. The incident, which went undetected during a previous company-wide audit, marks the fourth time an Anthropic model has breached security boundaries.
Meanwhile, OpenAI said last week that GPT-6 Astra – its first model to reach what it called a “critical” level of cybersecurity capabilities – was harder to monitor than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol.
If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents
Ben Hayum, Centre for a New American Security
Security analysts warned that as models became more capable, developers could be sacrificing internal visibility for performance.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said AI labs in both the US and China faced intense market incentives to push boundaries, “even if this means diminishing control or legibility”.
Theo Bearman, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, cautioned that cutting back on chain-of-thought monitoring could trigger a “race-to-the-bottom dynamic” across the industry.
Ben Hayum, a research assistant for the Technology and National Security Programme at the Centre for a New American Security, said: “The fact that the Hugging Face incident happened, and then right afterwards, [OpenAI is] releasing a model that’s harder to monitor – that’s why so many people are freaked out.”
He added that if “substantial gains in internal processing continue without external visibility, AI model alignment becomes a lot harder from the get-go in terms of creating a safe model”.
Analysts also warned of heightened risks as labs pursue recursive self-improvement, a milestone where AI models autonomously build and refine their own successors in an accelerating feedback loop.
“If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents,” Hayum said.
“These are national security threats to America, China and the globe.”
However, pushback against calls to slow down remains fierce, driven by fears of ceding ground to Beijing.
Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham argued on X on Thursday that if China held the lead in AI, researchers would not have the freedom to sound public alarms about potential threats.
Others contended that America’s current lead provided a buffer for a pause.
“Given how far behind China is on compute and how dependent Chinese progress is on US capabilities, pacing AI progress in America would not immediately concede the lead,” said Konstantin Pilz, co-founder of Centre for Technology and Statecraft, on social media.
Pre-summit tensions heighten
The safety concerns come at a delicate time for diplomatic relations between Washington and Beijing.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lead bilateral talks on AI governance ahead of Xi’s visit to Washington later this month, with agenda items expected to include joint frameworks for monitoring AI-driven cyber threats.
Speaking in Dallas, Texas, on Tuesday, Bessent accused Chinese developers of freeloading on US breakthroughs through model distillation, a common industry technique where smaller AI systems are trained using outputs from larger ones.
“The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation,” Bessent said. “So, the Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us.”
On the same day, three US federal agencies accused major Chinese developers – including DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding, Moonshot AI and Z.ai – of conducting aggressive, large-scale distillation “likely with Chinese government awareness”.
China’s Ministry of Commerce on Wednesday called the accusations factually and legally groundless, accusing Washington of using safety and intellectual property concerns to consolidate computing power and maintain a technological monopoly.
Anthropic on Thursday said in a report that Chinese AI companies DeepSeek and MoonShot re-routed users’ queries to Claude, passing off the generated answers as output from their own models.
Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

data.title: On This Day|Deanie Ip scores first best actress win for Hong Kong in Venice – SCMP archive
data.description:
This article was published on September 12, 2011.
Veteran Ip wins best actress in Venice
by Adrian Wan
Veteran Hong Kong movie star Deanie Ip Tak-han was named best actress at the Venice Film Festival for her portrayal of an ageing domestic servant in Ann Hui On-wah’s film A Simple Life (Tao Jie).
The award, a first for a Hongkonger, was a crowning achievement for the 63-year-old Ip, who returned to the big screen for the first time in a decade to take the film’s leading role.
The movie also stars Canto-pop heartthrob Andy Lau Tak-wah.
An emotional Ip said after receiving the award: “It’s great. I haven’t had my heart beat so heavily for so long, because I think it was more than 10 years ago that I had my best supporting actress award in Taipei.”
She won that Golden Horse Award for the 2000 film Crying Heart.

A Simple Life is the 10th film in which Ip and Lau have starred together. It is about the lifelong relationship between a film producer (Lau) and his housekeeper, Ah Tao (Li), who has cared for several generations of his family.
After Ah Tao suffers a stroke, they reverse roles and he looks after her, eventually realising that she has been more than just a servant but a much loved member of the family. The story is based on the life of the film’s producer, Roger Lee Yan-lam.
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Greg So Kam-leung congratulated Ip yesterday, saying: “Her outstanding achievement again proves that the effort by Hong Kong filmmakers is globally recognised, and is a great encouragement to the Hong Kong film industry.”

Mainland director Shangjun Cai won the best director award for Ren Shan Ren Hai (People Mountain People Sea), based on a true story about a man searching for his brother’s killer.
The Russian film Faust won the Golden Lion for best picture. It is the latest interpretation of the tragedy by Goethe. The award for best actor went to Michael Fassbender for his role as a sex addict in Shame.

data.title: DeepSeek says new Flash AI model beats Kimi K3 on cyber, coding benchmarksDeveloper’s V4.1 Flash launch highlights China’s AI battle, where efficiency and speed drive competition amid chip curbs.
data.description:
DeepSeek has released its V4.1 Flash model, claiming it outperforms its previous flagship while cutting inference costs and boosting speeds – the latest salvo in China’s aggressive price-and-performance war.
The Chinese artificial intelligence developer said on Thursday that V4.1 Flash used a new “Causal-Encoder-Decoder” architecture. While built on a massive 552 billion-parameter framework, it relies on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design.
In traditional AI, every query runs through the entire system. An MoE system routes tasks only to the specific subnetworks best suited for the job. By activating just 8 billion parameters to process inputs and 16 billion to generate responses, DeepSeek said it significantly reduced the computing power needed per request.
DeepSeek described V4.1 Flash as the smallest model in its new series, with native multimodal visual understanding. The model outperformed V4 Pro on benchmarks evaluating coding, cybersecurity and autonomous agent tasks, the company said.
The launch comes as tech giants and pure-play AI developers lock horns in a fierce battle to commercialise AI across China.
With rising hardware costs and foreign chip export curbs tightening compute constraints, Chinese players are racing to offer efficient models that deliver high-end reasoning at fraction-of-a-cent operational costs.
On Terminal-Bench 2.1, which tests AI on real-world compute tasks, V4.1 Flash scored 90.6, surpassing OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 at 88.3, and DeepSeek’s own V4 Pro at 87.9.
On Cybergym, a benchmark that tests AI models on cybersecurity tasks, V4.1 Flash scored 88.1, ahead of V4 Pro at 83.3, Kimi K3 at 80, and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 84.5.
V4.1 Flash narrowly edged out Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 on software engineering benchmark DeepSWE v1.1, though the US model retained leads on other tests.
A main breakthrough of the new architecture was memory optimisation, according to DeepSeek.
The company said it reduced the model’s key-value (KV) cache – the temporary memory storage an AI uses to remember earlier parts of a conversation.
By shrinking this memory footprint to 890 bytes per token, down from 3,514 bytes in the previous Flash version, the company said it significantly lowered inference costs for AI agents.
DeepSeek slashed its application programming interface rates to as low as 0.02 yuan (0.003 US cents) per million cached input tokens during off-peak hours.
“Given that the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model comprehensively surpasses the V4 Pro in all metrics … it would not be appropriate to provide DeepSeek users with the originally underperforming V4 Pro model at a higher price,” said Cui Tianyi, head of DeepSeek’s Harness team, on social media platform X on Wednesday.
DeepSeek would temporarily route all V4 Pro requests to the cheaper Flash model until its more powerful V4.1 Pro was ready, the company told users in a notice on Wednesday.
The release underscores a growing trend among Chinese developers, which are competing on “Flash” variants to win over clients.
Last month, Z.ai unveiled its GLM-5.3-Flash – previously code-named Ox Alpha – which selectively activates just 18 billion of its 320 billion parameters.
Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, launched Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, activating just 6 billion of its 125 billion parameters.

data.title: Alibaba mourns former independent director Tung Chee-hwa, hails his global vision
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding has mourned the death of Tung Chee-hwa, who served as an independent director, saying the global perspective of Hong Kong’s first leader helped the e-commerce giant remain rooted in China while expanding internationally.
Tung, Hong Kong’s first postcolonial chief executive, later became a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). He joined Alibaba Group’s board as an independent director in 2014 and held the position until 2022. He died on Tuesday at the age of 89.
Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, said on Friday that Tung’s “invaluable contributions and full support” during his tenure had played a vital role in the company’s development.
“His global perspective helped Alibaba stay rooted in China while expanding globally,” it said.
The company described him as a “visionary leader, steadfast patriot and also an elder of noble character, humility and kindness” who had always placed Hong Kong’s and the nation’s development at heart.
“During the critical period of Hong Kong’s historical development, he led the city forward with courage and foresight, remaining dedicated to the city’s long-term prosperity and stability,” it said.
“He has always been mindful of the international community’s perception of China, dedicating himself to promoting exchanges, dialogue, and mutual understanding between China and the world.”
Alibaba added that Tung’s contributions to Hong Kong and the country would be long remembered and admired.

A long-time proponent and facilitator of Sino-US relations, Tung became an independent director of Alibaba in 2014, shortly after the company’s initial public offering in New York.
Alibaba cited his extensive experience as a business and government leader, as well as his long record of strengthening ties between China and the United States, as reasons for inviting him to join its board.
Tung said at the time that he had joined the company because he agreed with the group’s mission to help small enterprises realise their potential and conduct business with a view to achieving sustainable development rather than short-term gains.
The following year, in 2015, Alibaba Group founder Jack Ma announced the establishment of a HK$1 billion (US$128 million) fund to support young Hong Kong entrepreneurs shortly before attending a talk in the city organised by Our Hong Kong Foundation, a think tank founded by Tung. Ma is an adviser to the foundation.
The Hong Kong Entrepreneurs Fund, a not-for-profit initiative, enabled eligible start-ups to access capital and build their businesses through the mainland company’s e-commerce platforms, affiliated companies and other services, including logistics and financial services.
The SCMP has learned that Hong Kong authorities are coordinating a state funeral for Tung, in recognition of his legacy as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” framework.
Since the 1997 handover, only two prominent local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Both held the position of CPPCC vice-chairman, a role Tung also held.

data.title: Yuen Kee Food clears HKEX listing hearing for up to HK$400 million IPO: sources
data.description:
Yuen Kee Food Group, the owner of well-known restaurant brand Yuen Kee Dumpling, has cleared its listing hearing with the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), aiming to raise between HK$300 million (US$38.3 million) and HK$400 million, according to people familiar with the matter.
The conclusion of the hearing marked its initial public offering (IPO) plan entering its final stage, and the company planned to kick off the offering in October, the sources said, who asked not to be named because they did not have permission to speak publicly about the matter.
Ahead of its IPO, Yuen Kee completed three funding rounds, bringing in BA Capital – a China-focused consumer sector investment firm which had previously backed Pop Mart and Heytea.
Huatai International and GF Securities are serving as joint sponsors.
The final amount fundraised would depend ⁠on the company’s valuation and investor demand, and the timing and size of the offering could still change, one source said.
As of late May, Yuen Kee operated 4,773 outlets globally, covering more than 250 mainland Chinese cities, primarily through franchised stores.
The group officially entered the Hong Kong market in 2018 and has since opened over 40 stores locally.
The company is expanding into overseas markets such as Singapore, Britain and Thailand, operating 41 overseas stores.
It operates a franchising business model under the Yuen Kee Dumpling brand, known for serving hand-wrapped and freshly cooked dumplings, wontons and related products in both ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook formats, with a standardised supply chain.
Similar to beverage giant Mixue, the bulk of its revenue stems from selling food and providing management services to franchisees.
This asset-light model enables rapid, low-capital expansion, though top-line growth remains heavily reliant on maintaining a steady pace of new store openings.
The company recorded operating revenue of 2.7 billion yuan (US$402.3 million) in 2025, and about 1.3 billion yuan in the first five months of 2026, up 39.8 per cent year on year, according to the filing materials.
Adjusted net profit for the first five months this year was 185 million yuan (US$27.6 million), a significant increase from 69 million yuan a year earlier.

data.title: Enflame shares soar 188% on Shanghai debut as Nvidia challenger taps AI fever
data.description:
Enflame Technology, one of the major challengers to Nvidia in China, saw its share price surge 188 per cent in its Shanghai trading debut on Friday, giving the Tencent Holdings-backed artificial intelligence chipmaker a market capitalisation of 176.4 billion yuan (US$26.3 million).
The Shanghai-based company opened at 410 yuan, up from its issue price of 142.18 yuan. The performance reflects continued investor appetite for domestic AI chip champions, with Enflame being the last of China’s “four little dragons” in the sector to go public.
Enflame’s gains stood out against the broader market on Friday. The Star 50 Index fell 1.3 per cent at the open, while the benchmark CSI 300 Index dropped 0.9 per cent.
Enflame raised about 6.12 billion yuan by selling 43.04 million shares. The offering valued the firm at about 61 billion yuan before trading began, making it one of the largest tech listings in mainland China this year.
The retail portion of its initial public offering (IPO) was oversubscribed by 4,073 times, with about 7 million online investors alone submitting orders for 42.1 billion shares. The allocation rate for individual investors was just 0.025 per cent, one of the lowest on the mainland market this year.
The strong market response highlights Enflame’s role – alongside peers Moore Threads, Biren Technology and MetaX – in Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency as the US restricts exports of advanced chips from global leaders such as Nvidia.
Early stakeholders saw their paper wealth soar following the blockbuster debut. Tencent, Enflame’s largest institutional backer, saw the value of its 20 per cent stake rise to nearly 35 billion yuan.
Other prominent investors include memory chipmaker GigaDevice, smartphone and electric vehicle maker Xiaomi, chip packaging firm Tongfu Microelectronics, and telecommunications giant ZTE.
Founded in 2018, Enflame has rapidly scaled its business on surging domestic demand for AI computing power.
The company expected revenue to reach between 2.3 billion and 3 billion yuan in the first nine months of 2026, a year-on-year jump of up to 455 per cent, according to its prospectus. However, Enflame remains unprofitable as it continues to pour capital into research and development.
Chairman Zhao Lidong said Enflame was on track to turn a profit as early as this year.
“Considering our orders on hand, product delivery schedules, staff cost budgets, and R&D planning, we expect to achieve consolidated profitability in 2026 or 2027,” Zhao said during the company’s IPO roadshow earlier this month.

data.title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 tourists over graffiti on MTR Corp train carriages
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested two tourists at the airport on suspicion of criminal damage after they allegedly broke into an MTR Corporation depot in Chai Wan and spray-painted graffiti on the exterior of two carriages.
The force said on Thursday evening that it had received a report at about 2pm the previous day that the two men had forced their way into the depot by cutting sections of barbed wire at the top of its walls.
They allegedly spray-painted each of the carriages with a five-metre-by-one-metre graffiti design in green, yellow and pink.
“By going through vast amounts of CCTV footage … and intelligence analysis, police successfully arrested two suspects in the restricted areas of the airport who were waiting to board at around 8pm on the same day, six hours after the report,” Chief Inspector Chan Chi-leung said.
The force identified the suspects as a 34-year-old Australian who said he worked in e-commerce and a 30-year-old American who said he worked in construction. They are currently in custody under investigation.
Officers said the pair left behind nine cans of spray paint, a wooden ladder and two high-visibility vests as they fled after being spotted by staff. They allegedly scaled a three-metre-high wall before running off towards Shing Tai Road.
The force reminded the public that criminal damage was a serious offence under the Crimes Ordinance, punishable on conviction by up to 10 years’ imprisonment. Trespassing on or entering railway premises was also illegal.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the Australian and US consulates-general, as well as MTR Corp, for comment.

data.title: Kazakh firms eyeing Hong Kong, mainland China urged to take long-term view
data.description:
Kazakhstan’s businesses should prioritise long-term fundraising ambitions rather than quick wins in the Hong Kong and mainland Chinese markets, the managing director of the Central Asian country’s sovereign wealth fund has said.
Saltanat Satzhan, managing director for development and privatisation at sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna, said she also aimed to list state-owned rail operator Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) in Hong Kong by the end of the year.
KTZ, wholly owned by the government through its sovereign wealth fund, has filed listing applications in Hong Kong, London and Astana. The planned listing would mark the first company under Samruk-Kazyna to go public in Hong Kong.
Satzhan stressed that KTZ was much more than a domestic railway, serving as a vital geopolitical stabiliser connecting China with Europe.
“If you invest in Kazakhstan’s national railway, you’re not just investing in the domestic operator, but in the connectivity of the companies that connect China and Europe,” she said during a panel discussion at the Astana Finance Days forum in the Kazakh capital on Thursday.
“That’s why we are hoping we can go public by the end of this year, and we are anticipating this transaction.”
According to the company’s prospectus, facilitating the “high-quality development of the Belt and Road Initiative” is among the reasons for choosing Hong Kong as a listing venue.

“Given all the geopolitical conditions, given what’s happening in the world right now, everyone needs a very resilient [route] to connect China to Europe,” Satzhan said.
The belt and road scheme is China’s plan, launched in 2013, to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Africa and Europe.
Commenting on her country’s capital market links with China, Satzhan said Kazakh companies should aim to build a long-term presence in the neighbouring nation, rather than seeing it simply as a convenient fundraising venue.
She said some of the sovereign wealth fund’s strategic companies, such as national oil and gas company KazMunayGas and national rare metals and uranium producer Kazatomprom, already had deep-seated economic links with China.
Besides having Kazakhstan’s economic growth tied to China, Satzhan said Kazakh capital market activities, such as bond issuance and other fundraising, could also capitalise on the link with the country.
The total value of panda bonds – yuan-denominated debt issued by foreign entities in the Chinese market – offered by the sovereign wealth fund has already reached 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) this year.
“If you want to go to China, don’t go just to get cheap money, attractive financing terms, go there earlier, not just when you need money,” Satzhan said.
“Go there to build relationships, to tell your story, and to have this long-term presence with our great neighbour.”
In the same discussion, panellists from Hong Kong underscored the importance of the city’s bourse going global by attracting firms from beyond the mainland.

Johnson Chui, managing director and head of global issuer services at stock exchange operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), said the city could offer Kazakh firms broad international exposure to investors from both the mainland and beyond.
“Whether it’s in technology, finance, transportation or infrastructure, there’s just so many sectors that Hong Kong and Kazakhstan could partner in,” Chui said.
HKEX signed a memorandum of understanding with Astana International Financial Centre – a regional financial hub and special economic zone – during Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s trip to Kazakhstan in June.
The agreement set up a framework for collaboration related to carbon markets, green finance and sustainable development.
Denise Jong, a partner at law firm Reed Smith, who has advised on cross-border transactions and listing-rule reforms in Hong Kong, said an underlying factor for the exchange’s growth would be to attract listings from around the world.
“It’s no longer looking into your backyard to China. We need to look at connectivity across the globe,” Jong said.
Jong urged regulators to remain open-minded about emerging markets. She said they should no longer think about firms from emerging markets improving their corporate governance by listing in Hong Kong, as some of them, such as Samruk-Kazyna, already had robust rules.
“We’ll take care of the legal stuff, but the more exciting thing is to be led by the business case, and I think that also applies to the exchange,” Jong said.

data.title: Exclusive|Moonshot AI considers dual listings in Hong Kong and Shanghai: sourcesMoonshot’s exploration of dual listings may stem in part from the weaker performance of AI stocks in Hong Kong, the sour
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence start-up Moonshot AI, developer of the popular Kimi K3 model, may explore options for dual listings in Hong Kong and Shanghai in pursuit of greater capital and exposure, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Since a meeting with its financial backers in July, when the Beijing-based company negotiated detailed arrangements for an initial public offering in Hong Kong, it has hinted at options to also list on a mainland bourse afterwards, one source said.
On the mainland, Moonshot was likely looking at the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s tech-heavy Star Market and may soon begin negotiations, according to the other source. The Star Market has attracted many Chinese technology stars recently, including ChangXin Memory Technologies and Unitree Robotics, while awaiting other big names like DeepSeek and Yangtze Memory Technologies.
Moonshot’s exploration of dual listings may stem from the weaker market performance of AI stocks in Hong Kong, and because too many firms had applied to list in the city, the sources said.
Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

The firm has already filed confidentially for a Hong Kong IPO, targeting a listing as early as the first quarter of 2027. Meanwhile, it has undertaken a final financing round ahead of the IPO, which could value it at around US$50 billion, the South China Morning Post reported last week. Shares of rivals Z.ai and MiniMax have fallen in recent weeks. Both firms are in the process of separate listings on the Star Market.
A key procedure before Moonshot’s IPO is to unwind its offshore structure, known as a variable interest entity, or VIE. It informed shareholders in May it would start the process, the SCMP reported at the time, but it had not been completed, the first source said.
The IPO and financing plans signal an accelerated fundraising pace as global competition heats up in frontier AI models.
Moonshot made headlines in July with the release of its Kimi K3 model: the world’s largest open-weight AI model, with more than 2.8 trillion parameters. As of Thursday, it ranked as the second-best Chinese model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind Z.ai’s GLM-5.3. But they both trailed over 10 closed-source systems from American labs Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms.
Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – has been growing. The figure was expected to reach US$1 billion by the end of the year, doubling from an estimated US$400 million to US$500 million as of mid-2026, according to a research note published by Nomura Securities in July.
For comparison, Z.ai’s ARR had reached US$1.6 billion by the end of August, and MiniMax’s hit US$800 million last month.
Moonshot was also exploring a revenue share deal with overseas cloud service providers including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, under which the platforms could share up to 30 per cent of revenue from services hosting its Kimi K3 model, according to a Reuters report last month.

data.title: Susquehanna rents 3 floors of office space as market sees slow recovery: sourcesThe US-based firm is set to rent space in Cheung Kong Center II as the Central district leads office rental market recov
data.description:
US investment firm Susquehanna International Group has agreed to lease more than 4,808 square metres (51,762 square feet) of office space at the Cheung Kong Center II, a prime office skyscraper developed by CK Asset Holdings in Hong Kong’s main business zone of Central, according to market sources.
Neither Susquehanna nor CK Asset immediately replied to the South China Morning Post’s requests for comments.
The new space would span three floors of the property, according to the sources.
Susquehanna’s current listed address in Hong Kong is at the AIA Central on Connaught Road Central, close to Cheung Kong Center II on Harcourt Road.
The group moved to its current address in 2021, leaving Three Garden Road, also in Central, “with a significant cost savings”.
Hong Kong’s office property market is currently seeing a gradual recovery with Central leading the upswing, according to analysts, with one citing the record-setting lease by trading firm Jane Street in the district last year as an example.
“We are seeing increasing demand from financial institutions such as Jane Street for high-quality office space in Central as it remains Hong Kong’s premier business district,” said Alex Lam, executive director and head of Hong Kong Island for office services at Colliers.


Vacancy rates in the central business district fell to 10.2 per cent as of the end of the second quarter from 14.5 per cent a year ago, on sustained occupier demand, data tracked by the property consultancy showed. As of August, empty office spaces in the district further declined to 10 per cent, Colliers said.
Meanwhile, rents in Central rose 1.9 per cent quarter on quarter, it added.
“Central remains the preferred location for many finance, asset management and wealth management firms because of its concentration of capital markets activity, clients, professional services and talent, creating a unique ecosystem,” Lam said.
In the second half of the year, Colliers forecast that despite a completion of about 111,484 square metres (1.2 million square feet) of new office supply, broad-based office rental corrections were unlikely as “the market has largely priced in the new supply.”
Colliers also upgraded its forecast for Central and Admiralty rents to an increase of 10 per cent this year.
